name: Cosmetic leg lengthening (Precice nails)

card.summary: Height surgery using a magnetically lengthened nail inside the bone instead of an external frame; well studied for medical lengthening, with limited cosmetic-specific data.
card.aka: Precice nail, magnetic intramedullary nail, internal lengthening nail, cosmetic stature lengthening
card.note: Major surgery: complications reported include nail bending, nonunion and other problems; the Precice nail is a medical device approved for limb-length discrepancy, not a cosmetic product.

quick.overview:
The Precice nail is an implant placed inside the long bone after the bone is cut. A magnet held outside the leg remotely drives the nail to lengthen in small daily steps, so the bone gradually grows longer without an external frame. It was developed for limb-length discrepancy, deformity correction and bone defects, and it has also been adopted for cosmetic stature lengthening, where healthy adults seek extra height.

The published literature on Precice is mostly case series and reviews in medical patients, in both adults and children. A 2025 meta-analysis and a scoping review have begun to examine cosmetic lengthening specifically, including complications and the quality-of-life measures used.
quick.mechanism: After the femur or tibia is cut, a telescoping intramedullary nail is fixed inside the canal. An external remote control with a magnet makes the nail lengthen by a small controlled amount per day, producing new bone through distraction osteogenesis. Orthopaedic papers evaluating the device report the distraction is accurate and the bone heals well, with the nail also able to shorten when needed.
quick.risks: Reported problems include nail bending or deformation under load, failure of the bone to heal, joint stiffness and other complications; some failures have been attributed to excessive loading of the limb. Surgeons describe the procedure as demanding, with weeks to months of limited weight-bearing and rehabilitation. Cosmetic use is elective and falls outside the device's usual medical indications.

lead: The Precice nail is a motorless, magnetically driven intramedullary (inside-the-bone) lengthening nail made by Ellipse Technologies, later NuVasive. An external remote control uses a magnet to lengthen the implant in small controlled increments after the bone has been cut, so the bone grows longer through distraction osteogenesis without an external fixator.[1][2] A 2014 study of the device noted that earlier internal lengthening designs had imprecise distraction, with nerve injuries, joint contractures and nonunion, and that the magnet-operated Precice nail had recently been cleared by the FDA.[3]

The nail is used for limb-length discrepancy, deformity correction, humeral lengthening and bone transport after tumour resection, and is also used in cosmetic stature lengthening.[4][5][6] Expert commentary describes strong bone healing with the retrograde femoral nail, and attributes the few failures to excessive loading of the limb and implant.[7]

Cosmetic lengthening is a smaller part of the literature. A 2025 meta-analysis compared external fixation with intramedullary nailing for cosmetic lengthening in terms of complications and functional outcomes, and a 2025 scoping review found that existing studies capture clinical results better than patient-centred life-impact outcomes.[8][9]

paras: After a precise bone cut (osteotomy), the nail is fixed inside the medullary canal with interlocking screws. Lengthening is performed gradually by an external remote controller; the 2014 evaluation assessed the accuracy and precision of distraction, effects on alignment and other outcomes.[3] The nail can also be shortened by remote control, a feature used in a case report to extend total lengthening in a 14 cm discrepancy.[10]

Surgeons often combine the nail with blocking screws and temporary external fixation to correct alignment, and a 2018 series of 27 patients describes combining an external fixator with the retrograde Precice nail for simultaneous acute deformity correction and gradual lengthening.[7][11]

Medical uses described in the literature include femoral and tibial lengthening in adults and children, treatment of limb-length discrepancy in fibular hemimelia (including combination with ACL reconstruction), humeral lengthening and bone-transport reconstruction after tumour resection.[4][5][12][13][14]

Cosmetic stature lengthening is performed for people of typical height who wish to be taller. Reviews of the cosmetic literature compare nails with external fixators and describe the older Ilizarov cosmetic experience, which a 54-patient series reported achieving a mean 7 cm of lengthening with improvement in psychological problems linked to short stature.[8][9][15]

A 2021 systematic review of Precice in children and adolescents included five studies with 131 patients and 135 femurs, evaluating clinical and radiological outcomes and complications.[2] A 50-case paediatric series from a single institution and other retrospective series report outcomes in adults and young patients, and a 2020 paper reports results of the nail for adult limb-length discrepancy.[16][5]
Expert commentary credits the retrograde nail with strong bone healing after femoral osteotomy.[7]

Reported issues include nail bending and plastic deformity, studied in a 2024 paper on femoral lengthening, and the retrieval analysis of explanted Precice systems, which examined device wear and failure modes.[17][18] Expert accounts attribute the few failures to excessive loading of the femur and implant during treatment.[7]

Earlier internal lengthening devices were associated with imprecise distraction, nerve injury, joint contracture and nonunion, which the Precice design aimed to address.[3] Cosmetic-specific complication rates are the subject of a 2025 meta-analysis.[8]

Published evidence consists of case series, reviews and technical notes. A 2025 meta-analysis of cosmetic limb lengthening compared external fixation and intramedullary nailing for complications and functional outcomes;[8] a 2025 scoping review of 20 studies mapped outcome measures in cosmetic stature lengthening;[9] and a 2021 systematic review covered five paediatric Precice studies.[2] Single-centre series report Precice use in 50 children and adolescents, 27 patients with combined deformity correction, and adult discrepancies.[11][16][5]
Registered studies include post-market evaluations of the Precice system in 32 patients, and ongoing studies in children and in adults with limb-length discrepancy.[19][20]

The device is discussed in height-surgery communities as the internal alternative to external fixators. Material specific to Precice in cosmetic use is limited in the sources reviewed for this article, so community claims are not documented here; see the Limb lengthening surgery entry for forum discussion of cost, destinations and recovery.
